title: RACE: Time Optimal Execution of Action Chunk Policies
one_liner: Speed up robot policies trained by imitation learning by replanning when to execute action chunks instead of just executing them faster.
lead: A robot learns a manipulation task by watching a person control it via remote. But the learned policy runs at the speed of those slow remote-controlled demonstrations. Simply executing the actions faster fails because the robot's motor speed is fixed and the policy's command was optimized for the old observation. This paper's RACE method accelerates policies by shifting to goal-position targets, replanning action timing, and searching test-time for controllable actions, achieving speeds up to 4x faster.

problem.h2: The speed trap in learning from observation
paras: A robot learns by watching: a person uses a remote control to pick up a cup, and the robot records actions at each instant. The trained policy — the behavior learned from those records — executes actions at the same rate they were demonstrated. But demonstration is slow: a person controlling the robot remotely is careful and deliberate.

Naively speeding up seems simple: just run the policy's output faster. But this breaks because real robots obey physics. When you compress the timeline (ask for the same motion in half the time), the robot's arm cannot physically move fast enough to reach the target — motors have speed limits, so the arm simply does not get there. More subtly, when you ask for an action command, the robot's current state (position, velocity) has changed since the policy saw the old observation; the command was optimized for the old state, so executing it now is wrong. These two problems — physical reachability and stale state alignment — pile up and cause failures.

callout.html: RACE replan when to execute action chunks, target desired positions instead of raw commands, and search test-time for actions that match the current state.

steps.b: Shift target from actions to states
steps.text: Instead of asking the policy to predict raw motor commands, retrain or reinterpret it as predicting desired goal positions the robot should reach.
Given a desired goal position, compute how fast the robot's physics will let it move and reschedule when each action chunk fires to reach the goal on time.

At execution time, if the policy's predicted action is misaligned with the current state, search a small neighborhood of actions and pick the one that gives the robot the most control (highest controllability).
Run the replanned, aligned action and read the new robot state. Loop back to predict the next goal.
The robot reaches goal positions faster without overshooting or losing control because actions are replanned to match actual motor speed and aligned to the current state.

paras: The paper shifts the learning target from raw actions (which are slow and brittle) to desired goal states (which work from any starting state and timing). It also replans when each chunk of actions fires to respect the robot's physical limits, and it searches test-time for actions most likely to work from the current state.

hidden.h2: Controllability: can the robot steer from here?
hidden.name: Controllability score
paras: Controllability is a measure of how much the robot can steer its motion from the current state given an action chunk. Think of it as the robot's "steering budget": how much room do you have to adjust the trajectory? High controllability means the action, executed from this state, lets the robot respond to corrections. Low controllability means the action will take the robot into a corner where it cannot easily adjust.

The paper measures controllability at test time by scoring candidate action chunks: for each action, compute how much control authority remains for the upcoming steps. Pick the action with the highest score. This way, even if the policy predicted an action misaligned with the current state, a nearby action with better controllability is chosen instead because that action leaves the robot more room to correct and adapt.

heat.caption: Darker means higher controllability. Starred states have the most room to steer.

reads.html: Imagine driving a car on an icy road. When you have full grip, you can steer and brake hard (high controllability). When you are sliding, you cannot steer (low controllability). You want to avoid sliding and pick actions that keep grip.
The paper computes controllability as a function of the Jacobian of the dynamics near the current state. Actions that leave the robot in high-controllability regions are preferred.

mechanism.h2: Why replanning + state targets + test-time search works
paras: When a policy predicts actions at demo speed, it assumes each action will run for a fixed time and the robot will transition smoothly. Speeding up breaks this assumption: physics does not speed up, so the robot cannot complete the transition. By replanning when each action fires, the policy respects the robot's actual speed limits instead of pretending they do not exist.

Second, targeting goal states instead of raw commands decouples the timing from the specific trajectory. A goal position can be reached via many paths and at many speeds. The robot now has flexibility: reach the goal in whatever time frame is physically possible. This is why actions generalize: the robot is not married to the demo's exact path.

Third, at test time the robot's state may not match what the policy expected. A misaligned action could fail. Test-time search solves this by ranking candidate actions by controllability: actions that keep the robot in a state where it can still steer are favored. This is a safeguard against distribution shift (when the test situation differs from the training observations).

math.words: Controllability score equals the minimum singular value of the state-transition Jacobian, multiplied by a safety margin. Pick the action in a neighborhood of the policy's prediction that maximizes this score.
symbols: Controllability score (how much the robot can steer)
How much the robot state changes per unit action (the Jacobian derivative)
The smallest singular value (the direction the robot steers worst in)
Safety buffer (ensures the robot stays in a controllable region)

bars.h2: Speed vs. success: the tradeoff solved

charts.title: Naive speedup
charts.note: Faster speed kills success rate because the robot's motor cannot keep up with the compressed timeline and the policy's actions no longer match the current state.

charts.title: RACE method
charts.note: RACE maintains success across 4x speedup by respecting dynamics and aligning actions.

items.html: If the learned robot dynamics model is wrong, controllability scores will be wrong and actions may fail. Real robots have friction, backlash, and delays the model does not capture.

If the policy was trained on slow demos and the test distribution (faster execution, different states) is far from training, the goal predictions themselves may be wrong because the policy never saw examples from the new regime and cannot generalize.
When the robot is near a singularity (a position where some degrees of freedom cannot move), controllability is low everywhere and test-time search cannot save it.
Train the policy on diverse states and speeds, validate the dynamics model on real robot data, and set the safety margin conservatively so the robot stays in controllable regions.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple robot simulator (e.g., a 2-link arm in PyBullet reaching a target). Train a policy via imitation learning on teleoperated demos at normal speed. Then run RACE: replan timing, target goal states, and search test-time for high-controllability actions. Measure success rate and time-to-goal across speeds from 1x to 4x.
demo.closing: The demo must show that RACE achieves near-demo success rates (>80%) even at 4x speedup, while naive speedup drops below 20% success.
